market_context: United States; natural cheese rinds and artificial coatings
title: Which cheese rinds are edible and which are not?

seo.title: Which cheese rinds are edible and which are not?
seo.meta_description: Natural, bloomy and washed rinds are usually edible; wax, plastic and other artificial coatings are not. Edible does not mean you have to enjoy or eat every rind.
seo.search_intent: Distinguish edible cheese rinds from wax, plastic and other protective coatings.

excerpt: Most rinds created during ripening — natural rinds, bloomy rinds such as Brie and washed rinds — are edible. Wax, paraffin, plastic, plasticoat and other artificial coatings should be removed. When the surface is ambiguous, the package label is the best guide.
content_html:
The outside of a cheese can be part of the food or part of the package. A white Brie rind belongs to the cheese; a red wax shell does not. The easiest way to decide is to ask whether that outer layer developed as part of ripening or was applied as a protective material.

Bloomy rinds: usually edible

The soft white surface of Brie and Camembert is formed by selected molds and microbes. It is edible and actively ripens the cheese from the outside inward, changing flavor and texture.

You can trim it for preference, but when it is the intended rind it is not unwanted spoilage mold.

Washed rinds: part of the cheese

Taleggio, Limburger and other washed-rind cheeses are repeatedly washed with brine or other solutions during ripening. Their orange, tacky, pungent surface is generally edible, although it may taste much stronger than the paste.

Natural rinds: edible, not always pleasant

Parmesan and many aged wheels develop a dry natural exterior as they lose moisture. If there is no non-food coating, that rind can be eaten, but long-aged rinds may be very hard or bitter.

“Edible” is not a command. You can use a hard Parmesan rind to flavor soup and remove it before serving.

Wax, paraffin and plastic: remove them

Wax, paraffin, plasticoat and plastic films are protective coverings rather than gastronomic rinds. Peel them away before eating. Cloth, leaves and other external materials may be used in aging or presentation, but should not be assumed edible simply because they touch the cheese.

When you cannot tell

Check the label for statements such as “rind not edible” or a description of the coating. For a store-cut wedge without the original package, ask the cheese counter.

A useful visual rule

An organic-looking surface that clearly developed with the cheese — dry, bloomy or washed — is often edible. A manufactured-looking, uniform waxy or plastic layer usually is not. The label overrides visual guesswork.

faq.question: Can you eat the white rind on Brie?
faq.answer: Yes. A normal bloomy Brie rind is part of the cheese and is edible.

faq.question: Can you eat red cheese wax?
faq.answer: No. Wax is a protective coating and should be removed.

faq.question: Is Parmesan rind edible?
faq.answer: A natural Parmesan rind is edible, though very hard. It is often simmered in soups or sauces for flavor.
